fatal_errors: The proposed rapid-supersaturation mechanism misses the central composition-dependent mechanism: Pt, Ir, or Ru first forms a lattice and dissociates hydrogen, whose reactive atoms reduce neighboring transition-metal species and enable their incorporation.
It cannot explain why Pt-, Ir-, and Ru-containing systems form single phases under the same mild treatment while Pd-containing and noble-metal-free controls segregate.

Suppressing atomic diffusion is asserted to promote alloying, although incorporation of sequentially reduced elements into an existing lattice requires atomic transport; simultaneous nucleation is neither demonstrated nor guaranteed when precursor reduction potentials differ.

The proposed supported-film and heating-ramp comparison does not reconstruct the spray-dried precursor particles, hydrogen reduction at approximately 300 degrees Celsius, or the relevant noble-metal identity controls.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad problem of homogeneous multimetal nanoparticle formation and offers a reasonably controlled, falsifiable fast-versus-slow heating comparison. However, it is a generic kinetic-trapping alternative rather than a reconstruction of the reported mechanism. It omits hydrogen-assisted sequential reduction, the distinct behavior of Pt/Ir/Ru versus Pd, formation of porous self-supported nanoframeworks, and Pt–Ru fcc-to-hcp phase tuning. Its predicted homogeneous-versus-segregated outcome agrees only at a high level. The proposed baseline does not use the decisive Pd-containing or noble-metal-free controls. Evidence E1 shows temperature-driven diffusion and segregation in a different Au-containing nanoparticle system but does not establish precursor supersaturation or rapid nucleation as the governing variable; E2 concerns bulk-alloy thermodynamics and is still less relevant. Thus the idea is testable but inadequately supported and inconsistent with the most diagnostic comparative evidence.
